A B S T R A C T
A series of low-density steels with alloving contents of C from 0.6 to 1.5%, Mn from 20 to 35%, and Al from 6.0 to
12.0% were fabricated in the laboratory. The microstructure, density and mechanical properties of the resulting
steels were examined to explore the effects of varving alloy content. The results reveal a significant influence of
alloy content on the microstructure of the low-density steels after solution processing in terms of ferrite phase
fraction, grain size, and κ-carbide size. It was found that the dependence of alloy density on the C, Mn, and Al
content can be formulated ρ = 8.1–0.102C-0.10Al-0.01Mn g/cm<sup>3</sup> (with the alloy content given as mass%). Both
the yield strength and the work hardening rate varied significantly with alloying content, where the yield
strength decreased with increasing Mn content, and increased with increasing Al and C content. The impact
toughness of the low-density steels was found also to be strongly affected by the alloying content, showing
Charpy impact toughness lower than 10 J for C content above 1.2%, for Mn content below 25%, and for Al
content above 10%. The effects of alloy content on the mechanical properties are attributed to differences in the
precipitation and coarsening of κ-carbides during the solution treatment process.

the lattice expansion and light elements addition, such as the element of
C and Al. Chen and Kim et al. [4,5] reported that every 1% decrease in

and Mn content leads to a decrease in alloy density by 0.101
g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 0.41 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, and 0.0085 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, respectively. However, the
densities calculated by Chen et al. [4] are lower than those reported
elsewhere [6–8]. As such, no accurate formula currently exists for the
calculation of density as a function of alloying content in FeMnAlC

effect of alloying additions on density. At the same time, it is recognized
that addition of alloying elements such as C, Mn, and Al has a significant

from several origins. One possibility, in particular for additions of Al and
C, is through solid solution strengthening [11]. Some studies have
shown that the yield strength can be increased by 30~40 MPa for every
0.1% of added C [12].

microstructure and phase composition of FeMnAlC steels, as well as
promote the precipitation of new second phases [10,13]. For instance,

tion and ordering of C and Al in the austenite phase [14,15]. In general,

amplitude modulation decomposition, which, in turn, influence the
precipitation of κ-carbides [16]. The specific size and spatial distribution
of the κ-carbides determines their impact on overall mechanical prop
erties. Based on the location of the precipitation, κ-carbides can be
loosely divided into intragranular κ-carbides and intergranular
κ-carbides [16,17]. In general, intergranular κ-carbides adversely affect
mechanical properties, while the influence of intragranular κ-carbides
on mechanical properties is closely related to the size of the precipitates
[4,18]. Finely dispersed and well-distributed intragranular κ-carbides in
an austenite matrix are beneficial for mechanical properties, whereas
intragranular κ-carbides of large size are typically not conducive to
improvements in overall mechanical properties. Ma et al. [18] suggested
that the addition of Mn may inhibit the formation of κ-carbides to a
certain extent, while Al and C may promote the precipitation and growth
of κ-carbides [19,20]. They related this phenomenon both to the sta
bility of austenite and to the driving force for κ-carbide precipitation. As
such, it is clear that alloying elements affect the precipitation of κ-car
bides, and thereby offer a significant potential impact on the mechanical
properties of FeMnAlC steels.

Despite the large number of studies dealing with the effect of alloying
elements on microstructures and mechanical properties of FeMnAlC
steels, most studies so far have been focused on tensile mechanical
properties, while only a few studies deal with the effect on impact
toughness of FeMnAlC steels. Moreover, there is still a lack of systematic
experimental data to allow accurate and quantitative analysis to support
alloy design of FeMnAlC steels.
Therefore, in the present work FeMnAlC steels with a wide range of
alloy compositions have been designed, and the effects of these alloying
elements on mechanical properties studied by changing the C, Mn, and
Al content. A quantitative analysis of both the resulting microstructures
and related mechanical properties under different alloy compositions
has been carried out with a view to guiding the design of FeMnAlC steels
with excellent performance.

content varying from 20 to 35%, and Al content varying from 6 to 12%
were fabricated in the laboratory. Each steel composition was first
melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace with a 50 kg ca
pacity, before being cast into an ingot with a diameter of 150 mm. The
resulting ingots, covering a range of compositions, were homogenized at
1200 <sup>◦</sup>C for 5 h, and then hot rolled into rods with a diameter of 16 mm,
before being air-cooled to room temperature. The chemical composi

3. Results
3.1. Mechanical properties and fracture behavior
Room temperature engineering stress-strain curves of the various
steels after 2 h solution-treatment at 1050 <sup>◦</sup>C are shown in Fig. 2(a–c). It
is clear that despite the similar heat treatment the engineering stress-
strain curves are significantly influenced by the variations in alloy
content.
As shown in Fig. 2(a). a strong increase in vield strength from 542
MPa to 1125 MPa is observed as the carbon content is increased from x
= 0.6%–1.5% in a Fe30Mn11Al(x)C steel. This strength increase is,
however, accompanied by a significant decrease in tensile elongation
from ~60% to ~20%, reflected also in a transition from work hardening
to work softening. The highest work-hardening rate was found for the
steel containing a carbon content of 0.6%, while rapid work softening
occurred in the steel with a carbon content of 1.5%.
In contrast, a decrease in yield strength, from 896 MPa to 401 MPa,
was observed as the Mn content was increased from x = 20%–35% in a
Fe(x)Mn11Al1C steel, Fig. 2(b). This decrease in yield strength was
accompanied by an increase in total elongation, from 28.5% to 60%, and
by an increase in work hardening rate. The variation in mechanical
properties with varying Al content was similar to that for variation in C
content. Specifically, the yield strength increased from 433 MPa to 846
MPa as the Al content was raised from 6% to 12% in a Fe30Mn(x)Al1C
steel (Fig. 2(c)), while the elongation decreased from ~75% to ~40%.
To reveal the influence of solution temperature on mechanical
properties, specimens with different Al content were also solution
treated at 1100 <sup>◦</sup>C for 2 h, again followed by water quenching. As shown
in Fig. 2 (d), there is a slight decrease in yield strength with increasing
solution treatment temperature comparing with that shown in Fig. 2(c),
which may be attributed to an increase of grain size with increasing
solution treatment temperature.
